paras: The lynching of Sandy King and Russian Bill was the hanging of two men accused of stealing stock by over a dozen masked men at the jail in Shakespeare, New Mexico, at about 2 a.m. on November 9, 1881. The two, described as members of a "noted cowboy gang" held for trial, were hanged from a joist after the mob seized their guard. A Tucson dispatch carried the story to papers across the country within a day, while correspondents in New Mexico and Arizona wrote of the hanging with approval or mockery.

According to a special dispatch from Lordsburg to the Tucson Citizen, the two men had "recently been arrested for dealing in stolen stock" and had been taken to Shakespeare for trial. A Deming correspondent of the same paper wrote that Sheriff Tucker arrested "Russian Bill," charged with cattle stealing, on the evening of November 8 and took him to Shakespeare in irons. The Tombstone Nugget, reprinted in the Los Angeles Herald, accused King of firing at an old man named Heenan while taking his horse near Soldiers Holes, and said a Lordsburg clerk shot him through the neck when he tried to take goods at pistol point. No report gave either man's race; the papers called them "cowboys" and "cattle thieves."

The Lordsburg special said that about 2 o'clock in the morning over a dozen masked men went to "the old Shakespeare jail," where the two were confined, seized the guard, and hanged both men to a joist until dead. King, it said, "died game," saying nothing in his own defense, while his companion "wanted to talk" and was "jerked up with his words in his mouth." That account placed the hanging at the jail itself, while condensed briefs said only that the men were "taken from jail" and hanged. The dispatch closed by remarking that "little sympathy" was expressed locally for the dead men.

The second man's surname appeared as Dittenborn in the Sacramento Record-Union, Littenborn in the Los Angeles Herald, and Littenbern in the Chicago Tribune, with the alias "Russian Bill" in the fuller accounts.

No report of an inquest, of arrests among the masked men, or of any official inquiry appears in the coverage. Instead, the Deming correspondent wrote that the citizens who carried out the hanging announced themselves "perfectly open for further engagements of a similar character."

Most papers learned of the hanging through a Tucson dispatch of November 9 that condensed the Lordsburg special, printed on November 10 as "Two Cowboys Hanged by a Mob" in the Chicago Tribune, "Lynching in Arizona" in the New-York Tribune, and "Cow Boys Lynched" in the Wheeling Intelligencer. Because of its Tucson dateline, the wire placed Shakespeare in Arizona, an error repeated in later briefs, and the Eaton Democrat put the jail at Tucson itself. Over the following week, weeklies in Wisconsin, Michigan, Ohio, Vermont and Mississippi ran one-sentence items, some without names, describing the dead as members of a "noted" or "notorious cow-boy gang."

In the West, the Lordsburg special, printed by the Sacramento Record-Union under "Judge Lynch in New Mexico" and by the Los Angeles Herald under "Cattle Thieves Lynched," described Judge Lynch executing the trial "in his own peculiar style" while calling the victims "luckless" and "unhappy." The Deming correspondent praised the hanging as done "with commendable promptness by the citizens." The Tombstone Nugget's sketch of King called his death a "neck-tie matinee at which he played as end man," and the Silver State of Nevada called the pair "cowboy desperadoes."

Accounts differed on the second victim: the Lordsburg special and the wire named Sandy King, while the Deming correspondent said Russian Bill was hanged with "his partner, a man named Ferguson" and did not mention King. The Tombstone Nugget's description of King as one of the cattle thieves "executed by Judge Lynch at Shakspeare" supports the King identification. Timing also varied: the November 9 dispatches put the hanging at about 2 a.m. "this morning," the Perrysburg Journal said "the night of the 8th," and the Deming letter, also dated November 9, had Russian Bill arrested on the evening of the 8th and brought to Shakespeare the next day.

bases: Over a dozen masked men seized the guard at the Shakespeare jail and hanged two prisoners held for trial on stock-theft charges (A2, A5, A4).

Two men were hanged until dead by 'over a dozen masked men' who overpowered their guard, an act the reports called 'mob-law violence' and the work of 'Judge Lynch' against men accused of stealing stock (A2, A5, A16).

The Lordsburg special (A2, A5) and the wire built on it (A4) are joined by an independent Deming letter (A16) and a Tombstone Nugget sketch (A17) that agree men were hanged at Shakespeare by a local group, though A16 names the second man differently.

framing.detail: Eastern and midwestern dailies ran the Tucson wire under 'Two Cowboys Hanged by a Mob', 'Lynching in Arizona', 'Cow Boys Lynched'.
The Lordsburg special treated it as 'Judge Lynch' executing a trial 'in his own peculiar style', calling the victims 'luckless' and 'unhappy' while reporting little sympathy.
The Deming correspondent praised the hanging as done 'with commendable promptness by the citizens'.
The Tombstone Nugget mocked King's death as a 'neck-tie matinee'; the Silver State called the pair 'cowboy desperadoes'.

conflicts.note: The 2 a.m. Nov. 9 hour and the 'night of the 8th' describe the same night; the Deming sequence is hard to square with a letter dated Nov. 9.
The Arizona placement follows from the Tucson dateline of the wire; the Lordsburg special datelines Lordsburg, N.M.
